doc: We are \⊤\ and \⊥\. \⊤\ is true. \⊥\ is false. \⊤\ is not \⊥\; \⊥\ is not \⊤\. This is how it is.
How do you make us? Just \⊤\ and \⊥\, nothing more, nothing less.
Some use the keyboard (/ctrl+9/ for \⊤\ and /ctrl+0/ for \⊥\). Some use the character search at the bottom of the @editor. Or you can drag us from here.
Check out our @FunctionDefinition below. They're very logical.
name: Boolean

doc: I evaluate to \⊤\ *only* when both @values are \⊤\. Helpful for determining if many things are all true. There are only four possible outcomes

inputs.doc: The other @Boolean to check. If the first is \⊥\, it doesn't matter what this is, the function will evaluate to \⊥\.

doc: I evaluate to \⊤\ when *either* @value are \⊤\. Helpful for determining if one of many things are true. There are only four possible outcomes

inputs.doc: The other @Boolean to check. If the first is \⊥\, the function will only evaluate to \⊤\ if this is \⊤\.

not.doc: I get the opposite of myself: if \⊤\, it gives \⊥\, if \⊥\, it gives \⊤\.

equals.doc: \⊤\ if both are \⊤\ or both are \⊥\.

conversion.number: Converts a @Boolean to a @Number, \1\ for \⊤\ and \0\ for \⊥\

doc: I can represent any text, from any @language. Just put the text between opening and closing text symbols: \""\, \“”\, \„“\, \''\, \‘’\, \‹›\, \«»\, \「」\, or \『』\.
To illustrate, consider these beautiful phrases
\“There are only two ways to live your life. One is as though nothing is a miracle. The other is as though everything is a miracle.”\
\『一日三秋』\
Just remember to close me if you open me, and use the matching symbol. Otherwise I won't know that you're done with your words.
\'hello'/en'hola'/es-MX\
You can also tag me with languages, and even give multiple translations. I'll evaluate to whatever languages are currently selected, if there's a matching language.
If you want to make me with some other @values, you can do this:
\"Here are some sums \1 + 2\, \2 + 3\, \3 + 4\"\
See how elegantly I just evaluated those sums, and placed them inside the @Text?
I have one last little secret: did you know we all have a unique number? It's true! You can refer to us by writing @U/ and our number. For example, @FunctionDefinition is 192:
See how @U/192 turned into @FunctionDefinition? I hear you call these numbers 'Unicode'.
Otherwise, there just so many glorious functions that @FunctionDefinition made for me to do all kinds of things with words!
name: Text

doc: I evaluate to the number of legible characters in the text; one letter is one character, one emoji is one character, etc. For example:
\'hello'.length()\
\'🐈📚'.length()\

notequals.doc: \⊤\ if I am /not/ the same character sequence as the given @Text.

doc: I make a new @Text that's me, with every letter in uppercase:
\'hello'.uppercase()\
Letters only have cases in some writing systems, so text in a writing system without them, like Japanese or Arabic, is unchanged.
My @language tag decides whose rules to use. Turkish has a dotted and a dotless i, and only text tagged as Turkish uppercases them the Turkish way:
\'iyi'/tr.uppercase()\
\'iyi'.uppercase()\
I make a new @Text that's me, with every letter in lowercase:
\'HELLO'.lowercase()\
Make two texts lowercase to compare them without caring about capitalization. This keeps every word that starts with an a, whether or not it's capitalized:
\['Apple' 'apricot' 'Banana'].filter(ƒ(word•'') word.lowercase().starts('a'))\
Like @Text/uppercase, letters only have cases in some writing systems, and my @language tag decides whose rules to use.
I make a new @Text from a piece of me. Counting starts at 1, and both ends are included:
\'hello'.subsequence(2 4)\
Leave the end out and I go all the way to my last symbol:
\'hello'.subsequence(3)\
I count symbols the way you see them, so an emoji made of several parts is still one symbol and never gets cut in half:
\'🐈📚!'.subsequence(1 2)\
If you ask for more than I have, I give you what I have.

inputs.doc: The place to start, counting from 1.
The place to stop, counting from 1. Leave it out to go to the end.

doc: I tell you where the given @Text first shows up in me, counting from 1:

If it isn't in me at all, I give @None instead:

\phrase: 'hello world'
phrase.subsequence(1 (phrase.index(' ') ?? 1) - 1)\

The @Text to put in its place.

And an infinite number of number/unit pairs…
I can be integers, real numbers, negative, positive, fractional, decimal, even not a number.
And you can write me with many different number systems, including Arabic \123\, Roman \ⅩⅩⅩⅠⅩ\, Japanese \二十\, and more:
You can also write me in bases 2 to 16 by putting a base number like this:
There is one special number called NaN that is possible when you write something that isn't a number:
There is no digit '2' in base 2, so it's not a valid number. NaN will also show up if you try to convert non-number text to number

doc: I'm a sequence of values, of any kind!
You can put anything in me: @Boolean, @Number, @Text, @None, even other @List, @Set, @Map, or any @expression. Here's a simple one:
\['apple' 'banana' 'mango']\
What makes me special is that I keep things in order and I number everything from 1 to however many items are in me.
My items are numbered, starting from 1. You can get values that I'm storing with @ListAccess, using their number:
For example, the second @value in this list is \['banana']\
\['apple' 'banana' 'mango'][2]\
I can have anything in me. Look at this list, with @Text, @Number, and @Time!
\['apple' 10 + 10 Time()]\

When you give me a list of many things, I'll generalize them if they have a @type in common. But sometimes you might literally mean those specific things. If you do, just put a ! after me, and I'll make sure that I represent a list of specifically only those values.
\['apple' 'banana' 'mango']!\
That's kind of it. But I can do all kinds of exciting things with my @FunctionDefinition!
name: List

\['apple' 'banana' 'mango' :['watermelon' 'starfruit']]\

\['apple' 'banana' 'mango'].replace(1 'kiwi')\

doc: I can take a list, and make a new list with its @values sorted. Like this:
I can also do it for @Text values, in alphabetical order. A capital letter sorts next to its lowercase one, so a word isn't sent to the end just for starting with a capital:
\['Orange' 'kiwi' 'Banana' 'apple'].sorted()\

And if you have a list of values that aren't @Number or @Text, you can give me a @FunctionDefinition that turns each item into a @Number or a @Text so I can sort it. For example, here we have a list of lists of different lengths; if you give me a function that turns each list into its length, I can sort by their length.
\[[1] [2 3] [4 8 12] [8]].sorted(ƒ(list) list.length())\
A function that makes @Text is how you sort by a word you compute, instead of by the value itself. Here I sort names by the last one:
\['Ada Lovelace' 'Grace Hopper' 'Alan Turing'].sorted(ƒ(name•'') (name ÷ ' ').last())\

doc: I'm a set of values! That means I can contain any number of values, including no values. You can make me like this:
I'm really good if you want to keep a collection of things without any duplicates.
That means that if you give me values I already have, I'll ignore the extras.
For example, this set has many duplicates:
I evaluate it to just \{1 2 3}\.
If you want to see if I have a @value in me, @SetOrMapAccess can help:
\{'jar' 'bottle' 'glass'}{'cup'}\
Usually, if you give me a bunch of values that are of a common @type, I'll assume they're a list of that type. Like this set is \{''}\, because it's all @Text.
\{'hey' 'hi' 'hello'}\
But you might want to indicate that I'm a set of /only/ those values, so I can tell you when you're trying to use one that's not allowed. If so, just add a ! at the end of me.
\{'hey' 'hi' 'hello'}!{'yo'}\🪲
Is there something else you want to do with me? Check out all the neat @FunctionDefinition I have!

doc: I bring values together, mapping *keys* to *values*. For example:
\{'amy': 6points 'tony':3points 'shiela': 8points}\
My keys can be any kind of @value, and my values can be any kind of value.
Some people like to think of my like an @index, or a dictionary, where you give me something, and I give you what it's mapped to.
If you wanted to check what something is mapped to, you can give @SetOrMapAccess, a @key and they'll give you the value:
\{'amy': 6points 'tony':3points 'shiela': 8points}{'amy'}\
If there is no matching key, I'll give you @None.
\{'amy': 6points 'tony':3points 'shiela': 8points}{'jen'}\
You can also make an empty map like this:
Usually, I'll see whatever kinds of keys and values you give me and just come up with a @type to represent all of them. Like this is a map from numbers to numbers:
But say you wanted to ensure it was specifically only those values; just add ! at the end of me, and I won't generalize. That'll help you know if you're trying to get a value you didn't intend.
I know how to many wonderful things with my pairings.

doc: \{⊤}\ if my pairings are the exact same as the given @Map's.

I'll make a new @Map with all the same pairings, but with the new pairing you give me. If I already have the @key, I'll pair it to the new @value.
\{'amy': 6points 'tony':3points}.pair('jen' 0points)\
I'll make a new @Map without the @key you give me, removing its pairing.
\{'amy': 6points 'tony':3points}.unpair('amy')\
I'll create a new @Map without any keys that have the @value.
\{'amy': 0points 'jen': 0points 'tony':3points}.remove(0points)\

inputs.doc: The @value to remove from me, along with any keys its paired to.

doc: Give me a @FunctionDefinition that takes a @key and @value and evaluates to \⊤\ if a pairing should be kept. I'll create a new @Map that meets your criteria.
For example, here we want to keep any pairings that are Amy or have more than zero points.
\{'amy': 0points 'jen': 0points 'tony':3points}.filter(ƒ(key•'' value•#points) (key = 'amy') | (value > 0points))\

inputs.doc: The @FunctionDefinition that decides whether to keep a pairing.

doc: Give me a @FunctionDefinition that takes a @key and @value and evaluates the value to a new value. I'll create a new @Map with the same keys but updated values.
For example, let's give everyone one point since they've been so nice.
\{'amy': 5points 'jen': 3points 'tony': 0points}.translate(ƒ(key•'' value•#points) value + 1points)\🪲

conversion.list: A list of the values in the @Map

doc: I'm a set of table rows! I can help you keep track of large collections of @values that have the same structure.
For example, imagine you wanted to keep track of a bunch of rocks:

\⎡name•'' color•''⎦
⎡'obsidian' 'black'⎦
⎡'pumice' 'grey'⎦
⎡'citrine' 'yellow'⎦\
@Bind can help you name it! And then you can do things like make a revised table with an new row @Insert:

\rocks: ⎡name•'' color•''⎦
⎡'obsidian' 'black'⎦
⎡'pumice' 'grey'⎦
⎡'citrine' 'yellow'⎦
rocks ⎡+ 'quartz' 'white'⎦\
Or if you want to find rows that match, you can @Select rows that match a @condition:

\rocks: ⎡name•'' color•''⎦
⎡'obsidian' 'black'⎦
⎡'pumice' 'grey'⎦
⎡'citrine' 'yellow'⎦
rocks ⎡?⎦ color = 'grey'\
Or maybe you want to make a revised table that has different values for rows that match a condition:

\rocks: ⎡name•'' color•''⎦
⎡'obsidian' 'black'⎦
⎡'pumice' 'grey'⎦
⎡'citrine' 'yellow'⎦
rocks ⎡: color: 'black' ⎦ name = 'pumice'\
Or maybe you want to delete a rows match a condition:

\rocks: ⎡name•'' color•''⎦
⎡'obsidian' 'black'⎦
⎡'pumice' 'grey'⎦
⎡'citrine' 'yellow'⎦
rocks ⎡- name.has('i')\
And if you ever want to get specific values from me, you can convert any table to a list and access individual rows with @PropertyReference

\rocks: ⎡name•'' color•''⎦
⎡'obsidian' 'black'⎦
⎡'pumice' 'grey'⎦
⎡'citrine' 'yellow'⎦
(rocks → [])[1].name\
name: Table

equals.doc: I check if I have the exact same @cells in the exact same order as another @Table.

notequal.doc: I check if any of my @cells are different or in a different order from another @Table.

conversion.list: I convert a @Table into a list of rows, where each row is a @Structure with its column names as properties.
conversion.text: I just convert a @Table to text.

Structure.doc: I'm a structured @value with named, typed fields, created from a @StructureDefinition. See @StructureDefinition.
name: Structure

equals.doc: I check if my @properties are the same name and @values as another structure's properties.

notequal.doc: I check if my @properties are different in any way from the name and @values as another structure's.
